title: Temperature and tokens
objectives: Change the temperature by raising probabilities to a power, and split text into tokens.

screens.title: Bold and safe
screens.prose: Two writers start from the row for “the”, and each has changed its chances in its own way. One writes boldly, the other safely.
screens.question: Tap the chart of the writer who picks “cat” more often.

hints.text: Compare the heights of the two cat bars.
Writer A's cat bar.
Writer A gives cat 0.75; writer B gives it about 0.37.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the taller cat bar.

byKey.right: Writer B gives cat about 0.37, writer A gives it 0.75.

explain.text: Writer A gives cat 0.75 and writer B only about 0.37. A is the safe writer: it takes the top word three times in four. B spreads its picks and writes more boldly.

screens.title: The temperature dial
screens.prose: Slide the **temperature** through $\tfrac12$, 1 and 2 and watch the chances for the row after “the”.

state.caption: Temperature 1: the counted chances, cat 0.5, the others about 0.17.

frames.caption: Temperature 1: the counted chances, cat 0.5, the others about 0.17.
Temperature 2: cat about 0.37, the others about 0.21.

screens.question: At which temperature does cat get its biggest chance?

options.why: At 1 cat has 0.5. Slide down to $\tfrac12$ and it grows.
At 2 cat falls to about 0.37: a high temperature flattens the chances.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read cat's bar at each stop.

explain.text: At temperature $\tfrac12$ cat has 0.75, at 1 it has 0.5, and at 2 only about 0.37. A low temperature sharpens the chances towards the top word, and a high one flattens them.

screens.title: Square and rescale
screens.prose: Temperature $\tfrac12$ squares each chance, then **rescales**: it divides each square by their total, so they add to 1 again. The squares are $\tfrac14, \tfrac1{36}, \tfrac1{36}, \tfrac1{36}$, which add to $\tfrac13$.
screens.question: Fill in the new chances of cat and mat at temperature $\tfrac12$, as fractions.

hints.text: Dividing by $\tfrac13$ is the same as multiplying by 3.
cat $3 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac34$; mat $3 \times \tfrac1{36} = \tfrac1{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide each square by $\tfrac13$.

byKey.no-rescale: $\tfrac14$ is the square. Rescale: divide by the total of the squares, $\tfrac13$.
byKey.no-rescale-mat: $\tfrac1{36}$ is the square. Divide it by $\tfrac13$ to rescale.

explain.text: Dividing by $\tfrac13$ is multiplying by 3, so cat gets $\tfrac34$ and each other word $\tfrac1{12}$. They add to 1, and cat's share has grown from a half to three quarters.

screens.title: Temperature 2
screens.prose: Temperature 2 takes the square root of each chance instead, then rescales. $\sqrt{1/2} \approx 0.7071$ and $\sqrt{1/6} \approx 0.4082$, so the four roots add to about 1.9319.
screens.question: What is cat's chance at temperature 2? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Divide cat's root by the total of the roots.
cat's chance before: $\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide cat's root, 0.7071, by 1.9319.

byKey.no-rescale: 0.707 is the root alone. Rescale: divide by the total of the roots, 1.9319.
byKey.squared: 0.75 is temperature $\tfrac12$. Temperature 2 takes square roots.

explain.text: $0.7071 \div 1.9319 \approx 0.366$, and each other word gets $0.4082 \div 1.9319 \approx 0.211$. The chances are flatter than at temperature 1: cat has fallen from 0.5.

screens.title: A tie stays a tie
screens.prose: The row for “cat” is sat, ate and “.”, each $\tfrac13$.
screens.question: What is the chance of “ate” at temperature $\tfrac12$? Give a fraction.

hints.text: Square each $\tfrac13$, then add the squares.
Squares $\tfrac19$ each, total $\tfrac13$; $\tfrac19 \div \tfrac13 = \tfrac13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square, add, then divide by the total.

byKey.no-rescale: $\tfrac19$ is the square. The three squares add to $\tfrac13$, so rescale.

explain.text: Each square is $\tfrac19$, and the three add to $\tfrac13$. Dividing by $\tfrac13$ gives back $\tfrac13$ each: a tie stays a tie at any temperature.

screens.title: More creative?
screens.prose: An advert says temperature 2 makes the model more creative, with new ideas of its own. Here is the row for “the” at temperature 2, with “sofa”, a word that never follows “the” in the text.
screens.question: What does temperature 2 really do to this row?

options.text: It flattens the chances; sofa stays at 0
It adds new words, such as sofa
options.why: sofa had chance 0, and the root of 0 is 0. Temperature only reshapes the chances the row already has.

options.text: It makes the model think harder
options.why: Nothing about the model changes. Each chance is raised to a power and rescaled, and that is all.

hints.text: What is the square root of 0?
sofa's bar.
0, so sofa never comes; the other words only share their chances more evenly.

feedback.correct: It only flattens the chances; sofa stays at 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow what the root does to each chance.

byKey.new: A word with chance 0 keeps chance 0 at any temperature.
byKey.think: Temperature changes only the chances, not the model.

explain.text: Temperature 2 takes roots and rescales, so unlikely words are picked more often, but a chance of 0 stays 0. A real model gives almost every token a tiny chance, so a high temperature lets rare tokens through; it still adds no knowledge. “More creative” only means less predictable.

screens.title: Temperature as a power
screens.prose: At temperature $\tfrac12$, square each chance and rescale; at 2, take square roots and rescale; at 1, leave the chances alone. $$\text{new chance} = \frac{(\text{chance})^2}{\text{sum of the squares}} \quad (T = \tfrac12)$$ The power is 1 divided by the temperature: $1 \div \tfrac12 = 2$ and $1 \div 2 = \tfrac12$. As the temperature falls towards 0, the top word wins every time.
screens.question: After “sat” the only word is “on”, with chance 1. What is its chance at temperature 2?

hints.text: What is the square root of 1?
1, and rescaling by a total of 1 changes nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the root, then rescale.

byKey.times: You multiplied by the temperature. Temperature raises a chance to a power, and 1 to any power is 1.

explain.text: $\sqrt{1} = 1$, and rescaling by a total of 1 changes nothing. A row with one certain word stays at 1 at any temperature.

screens.title: Temperature in code
screens.prose: `power` is 2 for temperature $\tfrac12$ and 0.5 for temperature 2: `x ** 0.5` is the square root of `x`. Round each new chance with `round(value, 4)`.
screens.question: Write `with_temperature(chances, power)`: raise each chance to `power`, rescale so they add to 1, and round each to 4 places.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each list is compared number by number with `math.isclose`.

mutants.symptom: Raises each chance to the power but never rescales, so the chances no longer add to 1.
Multiplies each chance by the power instead of raising it to the power, which changes nothing after rescaling.
Uses the temperature itself as the power, so it sharpens where it should flatten.

hints.text: Three loops: raise, add up, divide.
Append `round(r / total, 4)` for each raised value `r`.

feedback.correct: Your function raises, rescales and rounds.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: At power 2 the row for “the” becomes 0.75 and 0.0833 three times. Did you rescale?
byKey.test-2: At power 0.5 cat gets 0.366: take roots, then divide by their total.

explain.text:
Raise, add up, divide, round. Rescaling is the step people forget: without it the chances at temperature $\tfrac12$ add to only $\tfrac13$.

```python
for r in raised:
    result.append(round(r / total, 4))
```

screens.title: Tokens
screens.prose: A real model reads **tokens**, not words. A token may be a whole word, a piece of a word or one character. Here “unbelievable” is split into pieces.
screens.question: How many tokens does the model read for “unbelievable”, split like this?

hints.text: Count the cells.
Each cell is one token.
un, believ, able: 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each piece is one token.

byKey.word: As a word it is one token. Split into pieces it is three.
byKey.chars: 12 is the count of characters. These tokens are pieces.

explain.text: The model reads un, believ and able: 3 tokens for one word. Its next-token table would have a row for “believ”, and the likely next token there is “able”.

screens.title: Three ways to split
screens.prose: Split “an unbelievable rally” three ways, leaving out the spaces: into words; into the pieces an, un, believ, able and rally; and into single characters. Real models keep the spaces too, usually stuck to the front of the next piece.
screens.question: Fill in the number of tokens for each split.

hints.text: Count each split twice: once by eye, once by adding up.
Words 3. Pieces 5. Characters $2 + 12 + 5 = 19$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count each split again, leaving out the spaces.

byKey.spaces: 21 counts the two spaces. This split leaves them out: $2 + 12 + 5 = 19$.

explain.text: 3 words, 5 pieces and $2 + 12 + 5 = 19$ characters. The finer the split, the more tokens the same text costs, and pieces sit in between.

screens.title: Why pieces?
screens.prose: A table over whole words has no row for a word it never saw. A table over characters needs 19 tokens for our phrase. Most real models use pieces.
screens.question: Why pieces rather than whole words or single characters?

options.text: Pieces can spell new words, in fewer tokens
Whole words cannot be counted at all
options.why: Words can be counted, but a new word, such as a new firm's name, would have no row.
Characters spell anything, but a text then takes far more tokens: 19 against 5 here.

hints.text: What goes wrong with each of the other two?
Words miss new words; characters take many tokens; pieces avoid both.

feedback.correct: Pieces spell new words in fewer tokens than characters.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh what goes wrong with words and with characters.

byKey.spell: Characters can spell every word. Their cost is the number of tokens.

explain.text: A fixed list of pieces, which keeps every single character as a last resort, can spell a word the model never saw, such as a new firm's name. It also takes far fewer tokens than characters: 5 against 19 here.

screens.title: Drafting a contract
screens.prose: A chatbot's temperature setting works just like this. A law firm drafting a contract wants the same safe wording every time. After “The buyer shall” the chances are pay 0.6, and deliver and inspect 0.2 each.
screens.question: At temperature $\tfrac12$, what is the chance it writes “pay”? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Square each chance: 0.36, 0.04 and 0.04.
pay has 0.6.
The squares add to 0.44, so pay is $0.36 \div 0.44 = \tfrac{9}{11}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each chance, then divide by the total of the squares.

byKey.no-rescale: 0.36 is the square. Rescale by the total of the squares, 0.44.

explain.text: The squares 0.36, 0.04 and 0.04 add to 0.44, so temperature $\tfrac12$ gives pay $0.36 \div 0.44 = \tfrac{9}{11}$, about 0.8182. A firm sets the temperature low so the likeliest wording wins most of the time; lower still, it wins every time.

ideas: Temperature $\tfrac12$ squares each chance and rescales, sharpening the row; temperature 2 takes square roots and rescales, flattening it.
A tie stays a tie, a certain word stays certain and a chance of 0 stays 0 at any temperature in a table of counts.
A model reads tokens: whole words, pieces of words or single characters. Pieces spell new words in few tokens.

formula.name: Temperature $\tfrac12$
formula.note: Temperature 2 uses square roots in place of squares.

summary.trap: Squaring without rescaling leaves chances that add to less than 1; and a higher temperature adds no new ideas, it only flattens the chances.
